lessons.title: Get ready! What you will learn

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 🔢 **Strand 1 — Number**
Counting, calculating and reasoning with numbers — the language of trade, science and everyday life.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B9.1.2)
- B9.1.2.1 — Apply mental mathematics strategies and number properties to determine answers. B9.1.2.2 — Apply the understanding of the four operations on decimal numbers to solve problems and round answers. B9.1.2.4 — Demonstrate understanding of surds as real numbers, the process of simplifying surds, and determining (using a calculator) the approximate square root of a number that is not a perfect square.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- multiply and divide by powers of 10
- use the commutative, associative and distributive properties
- solve multi-step word problems and round answers to decimal places and significant figures
- identify simple and compound surds and explain the rules of surds
- simplify surds and approximate square roots of non-perfect squares

pages.title: Powers of 10 and number properties
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Multiply and divide given numbers by powers of 10 including decimals and benchmark fractions.
Curriculum indicator B9.1.2.1.1
## ✏️ Example 2.1
Find: a) 0.0472 × 10,000 b) 562.8 × [[1/1000]] c) 3.5 ÷ 100 d) [[3/4]] of 1,000 as a decimal of 10,000
**Solution**
a) **472** b) **0.5628** c) **0.035** d) [[3/4]] × 1,000 = 750; 750 ÷ 10,000 = **0.075**
**Indicator B9.1.2.1.2** Demonstrate the ability to determine the commutative properties of addition and multiplication.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Commutative property** — The **order** of two numbers does not change their sum or product: **a + b = b + a** and **a × b = b × a**. (Subtraction and division are **not** commutative: 8 − 3 ≠ 3 − 8.)
## ✏️ Example 2.2
Verify: a) 25 + 32 = 32 + 25 b) 17 × 8 = 8 × 17
**Solution**
a) Both give **57**. b) Both give **136**.
**Indicator B9.1.2.1.3** Use the associative property of addition and multiplication.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Associative property** — The **grouping** of three numbers does not change their sum or product: **(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)** and **(a × b) × c = a × (b × c)**.
## ✏️ Example 2.3
Verify and use: a) 15 + (6 + 9) = (15 + 6) + 9 b) (12 × 5) × 4 = 12 × (5 × 4) c) Find 25 × 37 × 4 quickly.
**Solution**
a) 15 + 15 = 30 and 21 + 9 = **30** ✓
b) 60 × 4 = 240 and 12 × 20 = **240** ✓
c) Regroup: 37 × (25 × 4) = 37 × 100 = **3,700**

pages.title: Example 2.4
pages.body:
**Indicator B9.1.2.1.4** Use the distributive property in solving problems.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Distributive property** — **a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c)** and **a × (b − c) = (a × b) − (a × c)**.
## ✏️ Example 2.4
Use the distributive property: a) 5 × (10 + 7) b) 5 × (10 − 7) c) 48 × 102 d) 6.5 × 24 + 6.5 × 76
**Solution**
a) 50 + 35 = **85** b) 50 − 35 = **15** c) 48 × 100 + 48 × 2 = 4,800 + 96 = **4,896** d) 6.5 × (24 + 76) = 6.5 × 100 = **650**

pages.title: Exercise 2.1
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 2.1** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. Calculate: a) 0.0089 × 1,000 b) 47.3 ÷ 10,000 c) 125 × [[1/100]]
2. Name the property used: a) 9 × 14 = 14 × 9 b) (3 + 8) + 2 = 3 + (8 + 2) c) 7(20 − 1) = 140 − 7
3. Use properties to calculate quickly: a) 4 × 87 × 25 b) 36 + 47 + 64 c) 99 × 45 d) 12.5 × 8 × 7
4. Show by an example that division is not associative.

pages.title: Word problems and rounding
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Solve operations involving addition, subtraction, multiplication and division using word problems.
Curriculum indicator B9.1.2.2.1
## ✏️ Example 2.5
A trader sells oranges from two baskets, A and B. Basket A contained 85 oranges and she sold 48. She sold 59 oranges from basket B and was left with the same number of oranges as in basket A. How many oranges were originally in basket B?
**Solution**
Left in A: 85 − 48 = 37. Basket B also has 37 left after selling 59.
Originally in B = 37 + 59 = **96 oranges**
**Indicator B9.1.2.2.2** Solve word problems involving the four basic operations and round the answers to two decimal places or to some significant figures.
## ✏️ Example 2.6
The price of a jacket is three times that of a shirt. A jacket costs GH₵560.65. Mr Mensa bought two jackets and four shirts for his twin sons. Calculate the total amount he paid, correct to α) two decimal places β) three significant figures.
**Solution**
Shirt = 560.65 ÷ 3 = GH₵186.8833…
Total = 2 × 560.65 + 4 × 186.8833… = 1,121.30 + 747.5333… = GH₵1,868.8333…
α) **GH₵1,868.83** β) **GH₵1,870**
> 🎯 **BECE tip** Do **not** round in the middle of a calculation. Keep full calculator values and round only the final answer.

pages.title: Exercise 2.2
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 2.2** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. A farmer harvested 1,248 tubers of yam. He sold 3 dozen to each of 18 customers and gave 75 tubers to relatives. How many were left?
2. A school paid GH₵14,756.40 for 36 desks. Find the cost of one desk and of 50 desks.
3. A car travels 412.5 km on 33 litres of fuel. Find the distance per litre, correct to 1 decimal place, and the fuel needed for 1,000 km, to 3 s.f.
4. Kwesi's monthly salary is GH₵3,875.60. He spends [[2/5]] on rent and food and saves 15% of the rest. How much does he save each month, correct to 2 d.p.?

pages.title: Surds
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Identify simple and compound surds.
Curriculum indicator B9.1.2.4.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Surd** — A **surd** is an irrational root of a rational number, such as √2, √5 or √12 — its decimal never ends or repeats. A **simple surd** has one term (√2, 7√3, 2√5). A **compound surd** is a sum or difference of surds (or of a surd and a rational number), e.g. √3 + √7 − √5, or 2 + √3. Note that √9 = 3 is **not** a surd.
## ✏️ Example 2.7
Classify each as a simple surd, a compound surd or not a surd: a) √2 b) 7√3 c) 2√5 d) √3 + √7 − √5 e) √16 f) 4 − √6
**Solution**
a), b), c) **simple surds** d) **compound surd** e) √16 = 4, **not a surd** f) **compound surd**
**Indicator B9.1.2.4.2** Explain the identities (rules) of surds.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Rules of surds** — **Rule 1:** √(ab) = √a × √b **Rule 2:** sqrt{[[a/b]]} = [[sqrt{a}/sqrt{b}]] **Rule 3 (rationalising):** [[b/sqrt{a}]] = [[b/sqrt{a}]]×[[sqrt{a}/sqrt{a}]] = [[bsqrt{a}/a]] **Rule 4:** a√c ± b√c = (a ± b)√c **Rules 5 and 6 (conjugates):** [[c/a + bsqrt{n}]] = [[c(a − bsqrt{n})/a^{2} − b^{2}n]] and [[c/a − bsqrt{n}]] = [[c(a + bsqrt{n})/a^{2} − b^{2}n]]
## ✏️ Example 2.8
Use the rules: a) √3 × √12 b) sqrt{[[25/49]]} c) [[6/sqrt{3}]] d) 5√2 + 3√2 − √2 e) [[4/3 + sqrt{5}]]
**Solution**
a) √36 = **6** (Rule 1)
b) [[sqrt{25}/sqrt{49}]] = [[5/7]] (Rule 2)
c) [[6/sqrt{3}]]×[[sqrt{3}/sqrt{3}]] = [[6sqrt{3}/3]] = **2√3** (Rule 3)
d) (5 + 3 − 1)√2 = **7√2** (Rule 4)
e) Multiply by the conjugate 3 − √5: [[4(3 − sqrt{5})/9 − 5]] = [[4(3 − sqrt{5})/4]] = **3 − √5** (Rule 5)

pages.title: Example 2.9
pages.body:
**Indicator B9.1.2.4.3** Simplify given surds.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Simplifying a surd** — Write the number under the root as a product with the **largest perfect square** factor, then use Rule 1: √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2.
## ✏️ Example 2.9
Simplify: a) √27 b) √72 c) √121 d) (√2)² e) √50 + √18 f) √48 − √12
**Solution**
a) √(9 × 3) = **3√3** b) √(36 × 2) = **6√2** c) **11** d) **2**
e) 5√2 + 3√2 = **8√2** f) 4√3 − 2√3 = **2√3**
**Indicator B9.1.2.3.4** Approximate the square roots of non-perfect squares with calculators or tables.
## ✏️ Example 2.10
Use a calculator to find, correct to 3 decimal places: a) √2 b) √5 c) √12 d) √30. Check one answer by estimation.
**Solution**
a) **1.414** b) **2.236** c) **3.464** d) **5.477**
Check √30: 5² = 25 and 6² = 36, so √30 is between 5 and 6, a little below the middle — 5.477 is reasonable. Also √12 = 2√3 = 2 × 1.732 = 3.464 ✓.

pages.title: Exercise 2.3
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 2.3** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. Which of these are surds? √8, √25, √0.04, √11, ∛27, 3√7
2. Simplify: a) √32 b) √75 c) √98 d) √200 e) 3√20
3. Simplify: a) √12 + √27 b) 2√45 − √20 c) √8 × √6 d) [[sqrt{72}/sqrt{2}]]
4. Rationalise the denominator: a) [[10/sqrt{5}]] b) [[3/2sqrt{3}]] c) [[2/sqrt{3} − 1]]
5. Without a calculator, find two consecutive whole numbers between which √90 lies. Then use a calculator to give √90 to 2 d.p.
6. Use √3 ≈ 1.732 to evaluate √75 and [[6/sqrt{3}]].

pages.title: Chapter 2 summary
pages.body:
- Commutative: order does not matter (+, ×). Associative: grouping does not matter (+, ×). Distributive: a(b ± c) = ab ± ac.
- Round only the final answer.
- Surds are irrational roots. √(ab) = √a√b; simplify using the largest square factor; rationalise denominators by multiplying by √a or by the conjugate.
